questions.stem: Which of the following is a non-electrolyte?
questions.explanation: Sugar is a covalent molecular substance that dissolves without forming ions, so there are no mobile charge carriers and the solution cannot conduct. The other three all contain freely moving ions and are decomposed when a current passes.

distractorRationale.a: Dilute acid ionises to give H+ and sulphate ions, so it is a strong electrolyte
distractorRationale.b: Melting sodium chloride frees the Na+ and Cl- ions, making it an excellent electrolyte
distractorRationale.d: Sodium hydroxide is fully ionised in solution into Na+ and OH-

questions.stem: During electrolysis, oxidation takes place at the
questions.explanation: Anions are attracted to the positive anode, where they give up their extra electrons to the external circuit. Loss of electrons is oxidation, so oxidation always occurs at the anode while reduction occurs at the cathode.

distractorRationale.a: Cations gaining electrons at the cathode is reduction, not oxidation
distractorRationale.c: Anions travel to the anode, not the cathode, because opposite charges attract
distractorRationale.d: Cations move towards the negative cathode, not the positive anode

questions.stem: When molten sodium chloride is electrolysed using inert electrodes, the products at the cathode and anode respectively are
questions.explanation: In the molten state there is no water, so the only ions present are Na+ and Cl-. Sodium ions are reduced at the cathode to molten sodium metal, and chloride ions are oxidised at the anode to chlorine gas.

distractorRationale.a: Hydrogen could only be formed if water were present, and molten salt contains none
distractorRationale.c: Oxygen would require hydroxide or another oxygen-containing ion, which is absent here
distractorRationale.d: These are the products from dilute aqueous sodium chloride, not from the molten salt

questions.stem: Concentrated sodium chloride solution gives chlorine at the anode, but dilute sodium chloride solution gives oxygen. The factor responsible for this difference is

options.text: the concentration of the ions in solution
the size of the applied voltage

questions.explanation: On position in the discharge series alone the hydroxide ion should always be discharged in preference to chloride, which is what happens in dilute solution. In concentrated brine the chloride ions vastly outnumber the hydroxide ions, and that overwhelming concentration overrides the normal order so chlorine is released instead.

distractorRationale.a: The same inert electrodes are used in both cases, so this cannot be the deciding factor
distractorRationale.c: Both electrolyses are carried out at room temperature
distractorRationale.d: Voltage affects the rate at which the products form, not which ion is discharged

questions.stem: In the electrolytic purification of copper, the impure copper is used as the

options.text: cathode, and it gradually grows thicker
anode, and it gradually dissolves away
cathode, and it gradually dissolves away

questions.explanation: The impure copper is made the anode, so it is oxidised and dissolves as Cu2+ ions: Cu -> Cu2+ + 2e-. Those ions travel to the thin pure copper cathode and are deposited as pure metal. Insoluble impurities such as silver and gold drop off as anode sludge.

distractorRationale.a: It is the pure copper cathode that grows thicker as metal is deposited on it
distractorRationale.c: The electrolyte is copper(II) sulphate solution, not the solid metal
distractorRationale.d: Dissolving is an oxidation, and oxidation happens at the anode rather than the cathode

questions.stem: Solid sodium chloride does not conduct electricity, but molten sodium chloride does. This is because

options.text: melting converts the ions into electrons
the ions are fixed in the solid lattice but become free to move in the melt
melting increases the charge on each ion
the solid contains no ions at all

questions.explanation: Conduction requires mobile charge carriers. In the solid the Na+ and Cl- ions are locked in fixed positions in the giant lattice and can only vibrate. Melting supplies enough energy to break down the lattice, freeing the ions to migrate towards the electrodes.

distractorRationale.a: The ions remain ions; no conversion into electrons takes place
distractorRationale.c: Ionic charges are fixed at 1+ and 1- regardless of state
distractorRationale.d: Solid sodium chloride is made entirely of ions; they simply cannot move
